statement: If two circles touch one another internally, and their centres be taken, the straight line joining their centres, if it be also produced, will fall on the point of contact of the circles.
heath_proof: For let the two circles ABC, ADE touch one another internally at the point A, and let the centre F of the circle ABC, and the centre G of ADE, be taken; I say that the straight line joined from G to F and produced will fall on A. For suppose it does not, but, if possible, let it fall as FGH, and let AF, AG be joined. Then, since AG, GF are greater than FA, that is, than FH, let FG be subtracted from each; therefore the remainder AG is greater than the remainder GH. But AG is equal to GD; therefore GD is also greater than GH, the less than the greater: which is impossible. Therefore the straight line joined from F to G will not fall outside; therefore it will fall at A on the point of contact.
ai_proof_text:
3.11
**Statement:** If two circles touch one another internally, and their centres be taken, the straight line joining their centres, if it be also produced, will fall on the point of contact of the circles.

**Step 1.** Let the circles ABC and ADE touch one another internally at the point A, the circle ADE lying within the circle ABC. By D3.3 the two circles meet one another but do not cut one another; hence A is their only common point, and every point of the circle ADE other than A lies within the circle ABC.

**Step 2.** Let F be the centre of the circle ABC and G the centre of the circle ADE [3.1]. Since the circles touch one another, they do not have the same centre [3.6]; therefore F and G are distinct points.

**Step 3.** Join FG [P1] and produce it in both directions [P2]. Since this straight line passes through the centre F of the circle ABC, it is terminated on each side by the circumference of ABC, and so it is a diameter of the circle ABC [D1.17]. Let H be the extremity of this diameter on the side of G, so that G lies between F and H. Thus G is a point on a diameter of the circle ABC which is not the centre (Step 2).

**Step 4.** I say that the straight line FG, so produced, falls on A. For suppose, if possible, that it does not pass through A. Since G is the centre of the circle ADE, the straight line GH drawn from the centre meets the circumference of ADE at a point D. By the supposition D is not A, and therefore D lies within the circle ABC (Step 1). Hence D falls between G and H on the straight line GH, and GD is a part of GH.

**Step 5.** Therefore GD is less than GH [CN5].

**Step 6.** Join AG [P1]. Since G is a point on the diameter FH of the circle ABC which is not the centre, and GH is the remainder of that diameter, GH is the least of all the straight lines falling from G upon the circle ABC [3.7]. Now AG is a straight line falling from G upon the circle ABC at the point A, and A is not H, because by the supposition the straight line FGH does not pass through A. Therefore AG is greater than GH.

**Step 7.** But G is the centre of the circle ADE, and the points A and D both lie on its circumference; therefore AG is equal to GD [D1.15].

**Step 8.** Consequently GD is greater than GH (Steps 6 and 7). But GD is less than GH (Step 5). Thus the less would be greater than the greater, which is impossible.

**Step 9.** Therefore the supposition is false, and the straight line joining the centres F and G, when produced, does not fail to pass through A. That is, it falls on A, the point of contact of the circles. Q.E.D.

*Path note:* the inequality AG > GH of Step 6 could also be obtained from the triangle AFG by 1.20 (AG + GF > AF = FH = FG + GH, and then removing the common part FG). The route through 3.7 was chosen because 3.7 gives the required inequality directly in a single step for exactly this configuration (a non-central point on a diameter), making the proof the most direct.
